title: Renal Clearance
subject: Medicine
summary: Renal clearance quantifies how efficiently the kidneys eliminate substances. It guides drug dosing, assesses kidney function, and helps detect acute or chronic renal impairment, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. It is calculated from urine and plasma concentrations and used to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
b: Clearance (mL/min) = (U × V) / P
U = urine concentration of the substance
V = urine flow rate (mL/min)
P = plasma concentration

sections.p: Kidney function is staged by estimated GFR (eGFR) using the CKD‑EPI or MDRD equations, adjusted for African ethnicity when available.
b: Stage 1: eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m² (normal or high)
Stage 2: 60‑89 mL/min/1.73 m² (mild reduction)
Stage 3a: 45‑59 mL/min/1.73 m² (moderate)
Stage 3b: 30‑44 mL/min/1.73 m² (moderate‑severe)
Stage 4: 15‑29 mL/min/1.73 m² (severe)
Stage 5: <15 mL/min/1.73 m² (kidney failure)

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, the common precipitants of reduced clearance are:
b: Dehydration from diarrhoea, malaria, or severe vomiting
Acute tubular necrosis secondary to sepsis, malaria, or herbal nephrotoxins
Obstructive uropathy from stones or prostatic enlargement
Chronic glomerulonephritis linked to post‑streptococcal infection or HIV
Hypertensive or diabetic nephropathy (increasingly seen in urban areas)
Sickle‑cell nephropathy

sections.p: Patients may have oliguria, fluid overload, or subtle rise in serum creatinine. In chronic disease, fatigue, nocturia, and anaemia are typical.
b: Reduced urine output (<400 mL/24 h) or anuria
Peripheral oedema, pulmonary crackles
Elevated serum creatinine and urea
Metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia in advanced disease

t.b: Estimates GFR; rising values indicate worsening clearance

sections.p: Rapid decline in clearance can precipitate life‑threatening complications.
b: Hyperkalaemia >5.5 mmol/L
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2)
Pulmonary oedema with respiratory distress
Uremic encephalopathy (confusion, seizures)
Volume overload unresponsive to diuretics

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, optimise volume status, and protect remaining renal function.
b: Rehydrate cautiously with isotonic saline if dehydration is the primary issue
Treat infections promptly: artesunate for severe malaria, ceftriaxone for sepsis, anti‑TB drugs for renal TB
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, high‑dose vancomycin)
Use loop diuretics (furosemide) for volume overload only after assessing volume status
Consider renal replacement (dialysis) when eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² with refractory complications

sections.p: Regular monitoring of renal function and modifiable risk factors reduces progression.
b: Check serum creatinine and urine output at least weekly in acute settings
Control blood pressure (<130/80 mmHg) with ACE inhibitors or ARBs when not contraindicated
Screen for proteinuria annually in high‑risk groups (HIV, diabetes, sickle cell)
Educate patients on avoiding herbal nephrotoxins and proper hydration

sections.p: Clearance is frequently mixed up with:
b: Glomerular filtration rate – GFR is a component of clearance but not identical
Pulmonary clearance – refers to removal of gases from the lungs, unrelated to renal function

sections.p: Certain conditions may give falsely normal or abnormal clearance estimates.
b: Low muscle mass (malnutrition, HIV) lowers creatinine, over‑estimating GFR
High protein intake or recent meat meals raise creatinine, under‑estimating GFR
Pregnancy increases GFR; standard equations may over‑estimate impairment

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden anuria or urine <100 mL/24 h

faq.q: Why is creatinine used to estimate clearance?
faq.a: Creatinine is produced at a relatively constant rate and freely filtered, making it a practical surrogate for GFR.

faq.q: Can I rely on a single creatinine reading?
faq.a: No; trends over 48‑72 h are needed to distinguish acute from chronic changes.

faq.q: What if the lab cannot measure urine flow?
faq.a: Estimate flow by timing a known volume collection or using bedside visual assessment; document the method.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with oliguria; what is the next immediate step? — Assess volume status, give cautious isotonic fluids, and obtain serum creatinine.
How does severe dehydration affect creatinine‑based eGFR? — It raises serum creatinine, falsely suggesting lower clearance; re‑hydrate before re‑calculating.
Which drug should be avoided in a patient with rising creatinine and why? — NSAIDs, because they reduce renal prostaglandins and worsen clearance.
Differentiate acute tubular necrosis from pre‑renal azotaemia using urine studies. — ATN shows urine Na >20 mmol/L, FeNa >2%; pre‑renal shows Na <20 mmol/L, FeNa <1%.
When is dialysis indicated in acute kidney injury in a low‑resource setting? — Refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics, or uremic symptoms.
Why might a malnourished HIV patient have a normal creatinine despite severe renal disease? — Low muscle mass reduces creatinine production, over‑estimating clearance.
Explain the rationale for using ACE inhibitors in chronic kidney disease. — They lower intraglomerular pressure, slowing progression, provided potassium is monitored.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a patient with chronic kidney disease? — New onset confusion or seizures indicating uremic encephalopathy.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect focused history and perform systematic exam to identify renal dysfunction and its cause.
b: History: onset, duration, fluid intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, malaria, TB, HIV, herbal meds, NSAIDs, recent antibiotics, blood transfusion, surgery, trauma, fever, weight loss, hypertension, diabetes, pregnancy, family renal disease

Examination: vital signs (BP, pulse, temp), general appearance (fatigue, pallor, oedema), abdominal inspection (ascites, distension), percussion (flank dullness, shifting dullness), auscultation (renal bruits), skin (petechiae, rashes), peripheral pulses, neuro (sensory loss), respiratory (crackles)

t.b: Measures oliguria/anuria; <200 mL/24 h suggests severe AKI
Indicates fluid overload; may precede pulmonary oedema
Suggests pulmonary congestion secondary to renal failure
Hypertension may be primary or secondary to renal disease

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use laboratory and imaging tests to quantify clearance, differentiate pre‑renal from intrinsic AKI, and guide management.
b: Serum creatinine & urea – rising trend indicates worsening renal function
Urine sodium & FeNa – FeNa <1 % pre‑renal, >1 % ATN
Urine osmolality – >500 mOsm/kg pre‑renal, <350 mOsm/kg ATN
Urine sediment – muddy brown casts = ATN
Urine protein/creatinine ratio – >0.5 g/g indicates significant proteinuria
Serum electrolytes – hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes requires urgent dialysis
Serum bicarbonate – <22 mmol/L indicates metabolic acidosis
eGFR (CKD‑EPI) – staging CKD
Ultrasound – hydronephrosis, obstruction, stone
Chest X‑ray – pulmonary oedema

t.b: Fractional excretion of sodium; <1 % suggests pre‑renal azotaemia, >1 % indicates ATN
Muddy brown casts confirm ATN; hyaline casts suggest pre‑renal
>6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes mandates urgent dialysis
<22 mmol/L with pH <7.2 signals severe acidosis and dialysis

sections.p: Apply standard criteria to classify renal impairment and decide treatment thresholds.
b: Urgent dialysis threshold – hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L or >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, refractory acidosis, pulmonary oedema, uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy

sections.p: A systematic ladder ensures safe correction of reduced renal clearance while preventing iatrogenic harm, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: 2. Identify and remove reversible causes: stop nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, amphotericin B), treat dehydration, correct obstructive uropathy, manage sepsis with appropriate antibiotics.
3. Initiate renal‑protective pharmacotherapy: ACE inhibitor or ARB if proteinuric CKD and blood pressure >130/80 mmHg; avoid if serum potassium >6.0 mmol/L or rapid rise in creatinine.
4. Optimize fluid balance: restrict fluids if pulmonary oedema, give diuretics (loop) if volume overload and adequate perfusion; monitor urine output hourly.

5. Correct electrolyte disturbances: give IV calcium gluconate for K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, insulin‑glucose for K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L, sodium bicarbonate if pH <7.2, consider dialysis if K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes or oliguria <200 mL/24 h.
6. Monitor trends: serum creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes, urine output, weight daily; repeat FeNa if unclear aetiology.

7. Escalate/referral: send to nephrology/dialysis centre when creatinine >3 mg/dL, K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, refractory acidosis, fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics, or oliguria <200 mL/24 h despite optimisation.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse effects and interactions guides safe prescribing in impaired clearance.
b: ACE inhibitors/ARBs: may raise serum potassium and cause acute rise in creatinine; stop if K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L or creatinine rises >30 % from baseline.
Loop diuretics: can cause hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, ototoxicity at high doses; monitor volume status and electrolytes, replace volume if signs of hypovolaemia.
Aminoglycosides: nephrotoxic; avoid or use therapeutic drug monitoring; discontinue if rising creatinine or FeNa >1 %.
Amphotericin B: causes tubular injury and hypokalaemia; give pre‑hydration, replace K⁺, monitor creatinine daily.
Metformin: risk of lactic acidosis when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²; reduce dose when eGFR 30‑44 mL/min/1.73 m², stop if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
NSAIDs: reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal perfusion; avoid in AKI or CKD stage 3b and above.
Herbal nephrotoxins (e.g., aristolochic acid): discontinue; counsel patients on risks.

sections.p: Prompt recognition of life‑threatening sequelae prevents irreversible damage.
b: Hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes → urgent IV calcium, insulin‑glucose, consider dialysis.
Metabolic acidosis pH <7.2 or HCO₃⁻ <22 mmol/L refractory to bicarbonate → dialysis.
Fluid overload with pulmonary crackles, SpO₂ <90 % despite oxygen → aggressive diuresis or dialysis.
Uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or severe pruritus → dialysis.
Persistent oliguria <200 mL/24 h despite optimisation → refer for renal replacement therapy.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local exposures modify presentation, investigations and treatment choices.
b: HIV: may have normal creatinine despite low muscle mass; use cystatin‑C‑based eGFR if available; avoid nephrotoxic antiretrovirals (tenofovir) when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
TB treatment (rifampicin, isoniazid) can cause interstitial nephritis; monitor creatinine weekly during intensive phase.
Malnutrition: low creatinine production leads to over‑estimation of GFR; rely on urine output and clinical signs.
Pregnancy: physiological GFR rise masks early CKD; avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs, use labetalol for hypertension, monitor proteinuria.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens tubular injury; control glucose, use SGLT2 inhibitors if eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m², avoid if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Alcohol excess: can cause acute tubular necrosis; counsel cessation, monitor liver function as co‑existing hepatic failure alters fluid handling.
Age extremes: elderly have reduced renal reserve, children have higher GFR per body surface; adjust drug dosing accordingly.

sections.p: Tailored approaches are required for vulnerable populations and resource‑limited environments.
b: Children: use creatinine‑based Schwartz formula for eGFR; avoid nephrotoxic drugs; fluid management based on weight percent dehydration.
Pregnancy: monitor serum creatinine (should fall), use protein/creatinine ratio for proteinuria; treat hypertension with labetalol or methyldopa; avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
Elderly: start ACE inhibitor/ARB at low dose, monitor potassium closely; consider frailty when deciding dialysis.
People with HIV: screen for HIV‑associated nephropathy; switch tenofovir to abacavir if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²; prophylaxis for opportunistic infections adjusted for renal function.
Low‑resource settings: when 24‑h urine collection unavailable, use spot urine protein/creatinine ratio; rely on bedside fluid assessment; use peritoneal dialysis if haemodialysis not feasible.

facts: Renal clearance = (Urine concentration × urine flow rate) ÷ plasma concentration (mL/min).
Hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L or >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, refractory acidosis, pulmonary oedema, uremic pericarditis or encephalopathy warrants urgent dialysis.
Oliguria <200 mL/24 h, anuria, hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, metabolic acidosis pH <7.2, or uremic symptoms trigger renal replacement.
FeNa <1 % indicates pre‑renal azotaemia; FeNa >1 % suggests acute tubular necrosis. Urine Na⁺ >40 mEq/L and muddy brown casts support ATN.
ACE inhibitors are started in CKD to slow progression; avoid if creatinine >3 mg/dL, K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L, or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
In low‑resource settings, amphotericin B causes nephrotoxicity via tubular vasoconstriction and direct tubular cell injury.
In HIV patients, low creatinine may mask severe renal disease due to low muscle mass; use cystatin‑C or eGFR equations adjusted for body size.

vivas.q: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with oliguria. What is the next immediate step?
vivas.a: Check serum creatinine, urea, electrolytes and urine output; start isotonic fluid resuscitation and consider early nephrology referral if oliguria persists.

vivas.q: How does severe dehydration affect creatinine‑based eGFR?
vivas.a: Dehydration reduces plasma volume, raising serum creatinine and falsely lowering eGFR; correction requires volume repletion before re‑measuring.

vivas.q: Which drug should be avoided in a patient with rising creatinine and why?
vivas.a: Amphotericin B – it is nephrotoxic, causing tubular vasoconstriction and acute tubular necrosis.

vivas.q: Differentiate acute tubular necrosis from pre‑renal azotaemia using urine studies.
vivas.a: ATN: urine Na⁺ >40 mEq/L, FeNa >1 %, muddy brown casts; pre‑renal: urine Na⁺ <20 mEq/L, FeNa <1 %, hyaline casts.

vivas.q: When is dialysis indicated in acute kidney injury in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Oliguria <200 mL/24 h, anuria, hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, metabolic acidosis pH <7.2, or uremic symptoms.

vivas.q: Why might a malnourished HIV patient have a normal creatinine despite severe renal disease?
vivas.a: Low muscle mass reduces creatinine production, masking renal impairment; cystatin‑C or eGFR adjusted for body size is more reliable.

vivas.q: Explain the rationale for using ACE inhibitors in chronic kidney disease.
vivas.a: They reduce intraglomerular pressure, lower proteinuria, and slow progression of CKD by decreasing glomerular hyperfiltration.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a patient with chronic kidney disease?
vivas.a: Sudden rise in serum creatinine >0.5 mg/dL in 48 h, severe hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes, or pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics.

vivas.q: A 45‑year‑old patient with an invasive fungal infection is started on amphotericin B. Renal function tests a week later show a rise in serum creatinine and a drop in creatinine clearance. What is the primary mechanism?
vivas.a: Direct tubular cell injury and renal vasoconstriction leading to acute tubular necrosis.

vivas.q: An asymptomatic 38‑year‑old woman is found to have mild hypercalcaemia and a very low 24‑hour urinary calcium excretion, with a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio below 1 %. What is the most appropriate management?
vivas.a: Diagnose familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia; reassure, avoid calcium supplements, and monitor serum calcium.

vivas.q: During axillary clearance for breast cancer, a surgeon accidentally injures the long thoracic nerve. Which of the following clinical signs is most likely to develop as a result?
vivas.a: Winged scapula with inability to abduct the arm above horizontal.

vivas.q: A patient undergoes axillary clearance and subsequently complains of sensory loss and numbness along the inner upper arm. Which anatomical structure was most likely injured during the procedure?
vivas.a: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (branch of the musculocutaneous nerve).

vivas.q: A 64‑year‑old man undergoes a subtotal gastrectomy for an antral gastric adenocarcinoma. To ensure an adequate proximal clearance margin in the unstretched stomach, what is the recommended distance of normal tissue required?
vivas.a: At least 2 cm of normal gastric tissue proximal to the tumour margin.

vivas.q: A 42‑year‑old woman is evaluated for severe upper abdominal pain radiating to her back. An amylase‑creatinine clearance ratio greater than 5 % is calculated; what condition does this finding help support?
vivas.a: Acute pancreatitis – the ratio indicates pancreatic exocrine dysfunction.

vivas.q: What does an amylase‑creatinine clearance ratio greater than 5 % typically indicate?
vivas.a: It suggests acute pancreatitis or pancreatic injury.

vivas.q: While inulin clearance is the gold standard for measuring GFR, what is the most utilized method in clinical practice for estimating GFR?
vivas.a: Serum creatinine‑based equations such as CKD‑EPI or MDRD.

mcqs.q: A 50‑year‑old man with chronic hepatitis B presents with serum creatinine 2.5 mg/dL and potassium 6.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the best immediate management?
mcqs.e: Hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L with ECG changes requires urgent calcium gluconate.

mcqs.q: In a patient with oliguria of 150 mL/24 h and serum creatinine 4.0 mg/dL, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
mcqs.e: Oliguria <200 mL/24 h warrants renal replacement.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman on amphotericin B develops rising creatinine. Which urine finding supports acute tubular necrosis?
mcqs.e: Urine Na⁺ >40 mEq/L and FeNa >1 % indicate ATN.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to ACE inhibitor therapy in CKD?
A 45‑year‑old HIV patient has serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL but low muscle mass. Which test best estimates true GFR?
mcqs.e: Cystatin‑C is independent of muscle mass.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most common precipitant of acute kidney injury in a low‑resource setting?

mistakes: Assuming serum creatinine alone reflects renal function in malnourished patients.
Using FeNa >1 % alone without urine Na⁺ >40 mEq/L to diagnose ATN.
Initiating dialysis only when creatinine >3 mg/dL, ignoring oliguria or hyperkalaemia.
Starting ACE inhibitors in CKD with K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L.
Treating hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L without ECG assessment.
Overlooking the need for volume repletion before interpreting creatinine‑based eGFR in dehydration.
Misinterpreting low urinary calcium as hypercalciuria instead of hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia.
Failing to adjust eGFR equations for African ethnicity in low‑resource settings.
